reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / standard rheumatology references
clinicalPearls: An acquired late-onset autoinflammatory disorder defined by a chronic urticarial rash together with a monoclonal gammopathy, usually of the IgM kappa type
The characteristic urticarial lesions are typically non-pruritic or only mildly itchy and are neutrophilic on biopsy rather than allergic
Recurrent fever, bone and joint pain, and demonstrable bone abnormalities on imaging are supporting features
Lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, fatigue, and weight loss may occur
Marked elevation of inflammatory markers and a persistent neutrophilic leukocytosis are typical laboratory findings
The syndrome responds strikingly to interleukin-1 blockade, underscoring an IL-1 driven mechanism
Long-term surveillance is essential because of an increased risk of evolution to a lymphoproliferative disorder such as Waldenstrom macroglobulinaemia or lymphoma
Secondary AA amyloidosis can complicate long-standing untreated inflammation
reference.pathophysiology: Schnitzler syndrome is an acquired autoinflammatory condition in which excessive interleukin-1 beta signalling produces neutrophil-rich urticarial inflammation, fever, and bone remodelling. It occurs in association with a monoclonal (usually IgM) gammopathy, and although the exact link between the paraprotein-producing clone and the inflammatory phenotype is incompletely understood, the clone reflects an underlying B-cell process that may progress over time.
additionalDifferentials: Waldenstrom macroglobulinaemia or other lymphoplasmacytic disorders
additionalInvestigations: Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation to detect the monoclonal component
Skin biopsy demonstrating a neutrophilic urticarial dermatosis
Acute-phase reactants and full blood count showing neutrophilia
Bone imaging (radiography, MRI, or bone scan) for characteristic osteosclerotic lesions
Bone marrow examination and periodic reassessment for lymphoproliferative disease
redFlags: Rising paraprotein, cytopenias, or lymphadenopathy suggesting transformation to a lymphoproliferative malignancy
Constitutional decline (weight loss, night sweats) warranting malignancy workup
Unexplained bone pain with lytic or destructive lesions
reference.prognosis: Symptoms are well controlled with IL-1 targeted therapy and most patients maintain a good quality of life, but lifelong monitoring is required because a substantial minority develop a haematological malignancy over the ensuing years.
pitfalls: Treating the rash as ordinary allergic urticaria and overlooking the monoclonal protein
Failing to order protein electrophoresis in an adult with chronic urticaria and fever
Missing secondary amyloidosis in chronically active disease
